name: Newcastle upon Tyne
title: Newcastle UTM: Ship Thickness Gauging on the Tyne
description: Ultrasonic thickness measurement in Newcastle and on the Tyne: renewal survey gauging in drydock at Hebburn, hull structure on car carriers and OSVs.
h1: Ship Thickness Measurement on the Tyne at Newcastle
intro: The Tyne built ships for generations, and its riverbanks still hold a drydocking yard at Hebburn, offshore and subsea engineering quays, a vehicle export terminal and the overnight ferry to Amsterdam. Teesport, Sunderland and Blyth are close by. For a superintendent with a ship docking on the Tyne or loading cars at the Port of Tyne, we bring a team from India to take the readings that the docking, the survey or the charter calls for.

highlights.p: The Hebburn yard's drydocks take cruise ships, offshore vessels and government ships for refit and survey. We fit into the docking on the owner's side, gauging to the TM plan as tanks and holds are opened.

Offshore construction, cable and wind service vessels lie in the Tyne between campaigns, which is the time to crack-test crane and A-frame foundations and gauge decks and ballast tanks emptied for once.

highlights.h: Tyne, Tees, Wear and Blyth together
highlights.p: The north-east ports are close together by road, so a team mobilised for one ship can take in-service jobs at Teesport, Sunderland or Blyth on the same visit when the schedules allow.

port.h: Newcastle and the Tyne: shipbuilding river turned repair and energy port
p: Shipbuilding on the Tyne shaped Newcastle, and while the great building berths at Wallsend and Walker are gone, the river is still a working maritime estuary. The Port of Tyne runs a vehicle terminal that ships cars built in the region to Europe and beyond on car carriers, handles dry bulk and general cargo, and operates the North Shields terminal used by DFDS's overnight ferry to Amsterdam (IJmuiden). Upriver at Hebburn, a ship-repair yard with drydocks takes cruise ships, offshore vessels and government ships, and the riverbanks hold fabrication and subsea engineering sites serving the offshore energy industry.

Within easy reach are Teesport, run by PD Ports, with its chemical and process-industry jetties and container and bulk berths; the Port of Sunderland on the Wear; and the Port of Blyth to the north, with its offshore and renewable-energy quays. Together, the north-east coast of England gives a gauging team a cluster of berths that can be covered in one trip, which matters when a fleet has several ships trading into the region in the same month. Hull gauging in north east England is therefore planned as a regional job more often than a single-berth one.

Two things keep ships on the Tyne long enough to gauge. Drydock and afloat repair periods at Hebburn give the classic renewal-survey window, with tanks open and staging in place. And the energy sector keeps offshore construction and service vessels in the river between projects, sometimes for weeks. Car carriers and the ferry are quick, scheduled calls, but their regularity means a scope can be planned across several visits. Inspection demand is therefore varied for a port of this size: full survey gauging in dock, crack detection on offshore equipment foundations, and short-call checks on ramps and vehicle decks. Ship inspection in Newcastle upon Tyne rarely looks the same from one job to the next.

facilities.h: Yards, quays and terminals for gauging on the Tyne and Tees
p: At the Hebburn yard, gauging is planned around the docking programme. The yard's planners, the class surveyor and the owner's superintendent agree the TM plan, the team works through tanks and holds as they are cleaned and ventilated, and readings showing substantial corrosion go back to the surveyor and the yard as they are found, so steel renewal can be scoped while the ship is still in dock. Shell plating is reached from the dock floor, and the double bottom is usually the critical path.

On the river quays and at Teesport, work is in service. Car carriers at the Port of Tyne berth for loading and sail on schedule, so the scope is chosen for what can be reached in that time. Offshore and construction vessels lying in the river between projects can be gauged without that pressure, including the deck foundations for cranes, A-frames and cable carousels that see heavy cyclic load. Chemical tankers at the Tees jetties are worked within each terminal's permit system, which usually means deck and piping alongside and tank entry only in a gas-free window. Offshore vessel inspection on the river quays is the most flexible work in the region, because the ship has nowhere to be.
list: Hebburn ship-repair yard drydocks — a tank-by-tank TM programme run to the docking schedule, with findings passed to the yard while there is still time to renew.
Port of Tyne vehicle terminal — ramps, hinge lugs, hoistable decks and weather-deck plating on car carriers during loading.
North Shields ferry terminal — vehicle-deck, ramp and bow structure checks on the Amsterdam ro-pax, timed around the ship's port stay.
River quays for offshore and construction vessels — crane, A-frame and carousel foundation crack detection and deck gauging between projects.
Teesport and the Tees jetties — deck and piping gauging on chemical and product tankers and bulk carriers, under each terminal's permit rules.
Port of Blyth and Port of Sunderland — in-service gauging on offshore wind support vessels and bulk and general cargo ships.

context.h: Regulation and market drivers on England's north-east coast
p: Both rivers fall within the North Sea SOx Emission Control Area, where the sulphur cap is 0.10%. Car carriers and ferries on North Sea routes have worked to the 0.10% limit since it took effect in the ECA in 2015, and scrubber piping on the ships that fitted systems is now well into its service life. Port state control is the Maritime and Coastguard Agency's job here as elsewhere in the UK: the country left the EU but not the Paris MoU, and inspects on that basis under its own legislation.

The market here is driven by energy and by the region's manufacturing exports. Offshore wind farms off the north-east coast and in the southern North Sea bring construction, cable and service vessels into the river; the subsea engineering cluster on the Tyne keeps construction vessels calling; and car exports keep a regular stream of car carriers on the river. Teesside's chemical and process industries add tankers to the mix. The Tyne also has a long P&I connection: the North of England P&I Association was founded in Newcastle, and the club formed by its merger, NorthStandard, still works from the city, so condition questions on older ships are often asked here.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs in Newcastle and on the Tyne
jobs.p: Tyne work ranges from full survey gauging in dock to short scheduled calls. For yard jobs we agree the TM plan with the class surveyor; for in-service jobs we fit the scope to the ship's time alongside, using repeat calls where the ship runs a regular service. For vessels lying in the river between energy projects, a full tank and foundation programme can be worked through while the ship is idle.
list: Renewal survey gauging on the Tyne for a cruise ship or ferry in drydock at Hebburn, covering ballast tanks, double bottoms and sea-water piping, with findings marked for the yard.
Car carrier inspection on the Tyne during loading: stern ramp plating UT, MPI at hinge lugs and ramp-wire sheave foundations, and weather-deck readings.
Offshore construction vessel lying in the Tyne between wind-farm campaigns: magnetic particle testing of crane pedestal and A-frame foundation welds, with deck gauging alongside.
Thickness measurement on Teesside: deck, cargo piping and accessible tank gauging on a chemical tanker at a Tees jetty ahead of its intermediate survey.
Pre-docking steel estimate on the Amsterdam ro-pax, split across consecutive port stays at North Shields, ahead of its annual refit at a yard.

logistics: Newcastle International Airport is the usual arrival point, with connections through London and European hubs; Teesside International Airport serves the Tees side on a smaller route network. Yard, terminal and quay access is ISPS-controlled, and passes are arranged in advance by the ship's agent or, for dockings, by the yard. Our technicians travel from India on UK visas, so for docking work we lock in dates as soon as the yard confirms the slot, and for in-service work we use the ferry timetable or car carrier rotation to pick the call.

faqs.q: Do you work at the Hebburn ship-repair yard?
faqs.a: Yes, on behalf of the shipowner or manager whose vessel is docked there. The preparation happens before the ship reaches the Tyne: the TM plan is settled with the attending class surveyor, and the superintendent books staging, access and a tank-cleaning order with the yard. During the docking, areas of substantial or excessive corrosion are reported and marked as they are found, so renewal can be decided before undocking rather than after.

faqs.q: Can one trip cover the Tyne and Teesside?
faqs.a: Yes, where schedules allow. The Tyne, the Wear, Blyth and the Tees are all within reach by road, so a team mobilised for a docking at Hebburn can also take an in-service job on a tanker at Teesport or a wind vessel at Blyth. Each ship's agent handles its own passes, so we line up boarding times between them before the team leaves India.

faqs.q: Is thickness gauging useful for offshore construction vessels between projects?
faqs.a: Yes. Between campaigns a construction vessel's deck can be cleared and its tanks emptied, which rarely happens during a project. That is the time to gauge working-deck plating under heavy equipment, crack-test crane, A-frame and carousel foundations, and take readings in ballast tanks that are full for most of a campaign. Findings can then be repaired before the next mobilisation rather than during it.

faqs.q: Are North Sea ferries still worth checking for scrubber piping?
faqs.a: If the ferry is scrubber-fitted, yes. North Sea ferries have operated under the 0.10% sulphur ECA limit since 2015, and some owners fitted scrubbers to keep using heavier fuel. After years of service, the wash-water and overboard lines are due for a wall-thickness check, ideally before the annual refit so any renewal can be planned into it rather than handled as a defect.
